Day 36 of 100 · Infrastructure Automation

Ansible Handlers

#100DaysOfCloudAndSecurityInfrastructure AutomationPublished after ledger snapshot

Handlers trigger follow-up actions such as service reloads only when notifying tasks actually change something.

Architecture / mental model

task changes → notify → handler queued → handler runs at handler flush/end of play

How it works

A handler is typically used for actions that should only happen after a meaningful configuration change, such as reloading Nginx after its configuration file changed.

Multiple tasks can notify the same handler and Ansible de-duplicates the notification so the service does not restart after every tiny task.

Handlers normally run later in the play. That timing matters if later tasks require the new configuration immediately; use the design intentionally instead of assuming notification means instant execution.

Hands-on reference

# task: notify: Reload nginx
# handler: ansible.builtin.service: name=nginx state=reloaded

Verification

Run once with a changed template and confirm the handler runs; run again without changes and confirm the handler is not triggered.

Field note / gotcha

If a play fails before notified handlers run, the expected reload may never happen unless handler behavior is deliberately designed, for example with force-handlers where appropriate.

Security considerations

Validate configuration before notifying a privileged service reload. Automation should not efficiently reload a broken config.

What I learned

Change-driven actions are safer than unconditional restarts.
